title: Off Broadway Review: THE OTHER AMERICANS - Bored and Confused?
transcript: Hello. Welcome to Bored and Confused, where I review shows based on two criteria. One, was I bored? Two, was I confused. Today's show is The Other Americans Playing at the Public Theater. But before I jump into this, a quick reminder to please like, comment, and subscribe. It really helps me out and honestly, it makes me feel really good about myself. So, go ahead and click that button, leave a comment, and let's talk about some theater. So, The Other Americans is a brand new play by John Leguisamo. Now, I've been a fan of John for years, from his oneperson plays like Freak and Latin History for Morons to his film and TV work, but I've never seen him live on stage before this. And that made this production pretty exciting for me personally. This is his first multicaracter ensemble play. And that's a big step for someone so associated with solo performances. And I think that's worth celebrating right there. He's taking on a new challenge, stretching himself as a writer and really putting himself out there. Also, side note, I'm a big fan of Ruben Santiago Hudson's work. He's the director of this. I saw his one man play Lacawana Blues when Roundabout revived it a few years ago, and I was blown away by it. I found it moving. I found it incredibly theatrical. He was fantastic at it. So, knowing that he was directing this play also made me really excited to see it. This play first premiered at Arena Stage in Washington DC before coming here to New York. So what is this show about? This play is set in Queens, specifically Forest Hills around the late 1990s or early 2000s. The main character is Nelson Castro, played by Leguisamo himself. Nelson's parents were immigrants and he grew up in Jackson Heights. His father, when he passed away, left him and his sister Norma half shares of a laundromat business. And while Norma has become more successful, Nelson has been chasing a bigger dream. He's moved his wife Patty and their family out to Jackson Heights and into Forest Hills into a larger, more expensive house in a mostly white neighborhood. Now, the play opens with Nelson hustling on the phone trying to close some sort of deal. And then we start meeting the family members. Patty, his wife, who is loyal and supportive, but also has her limits. Norma, the older sister, is practical, more grounded. A neighborhood friend drops by and their daughter makes an appearance. But the real tension comes from their son, Nick or Nikki, who is about to come home after a long absence. And here's the thing, the play really holds off on telling us exactly why Nikki's been away. There's this suspense that builds slowly. It's revealed that while he was in high school living in that new neighborhood that they live now, he was brutally attacked, beaten nearly to death. And now that trauma has followed him into college where he has had a mental breakdown and was eventually placed in a facility to recover. Now he's coming home and everyone's on edge about it. So the first act is all about these relationships. Nelson wanting to move forward, Patty trying to keep the family together, Norma being sharp and judgmental, and Nikki needing to process his trauma, and the rest of the family trying not to talk about it. I thought the first act of this play was really strong. The dialogue feels natural. It sounds like real people in Queens at this time. Every character feels three-dimensional, and that's a credit both to Legosamo's writing as well to the ensemble cast who are doing excellent work. Truly, there isn't a weak link on that stage. The family dynamics are complicated, but believable. Everyone is struggling with their own hopes and disappointments, but they're also negotiating those dreams through the lens of family obligation. And that's a tricky balance to write and Leguisamo does it really well. And let me take a second to mention the set by Arnof Maldonado. It's not flashy, but it's really effective. It looks and feels like a real queen's house. The furniture, the layout, the little details, all of it grounds the story in reality. That realism made the tension between the characters hit even harder because it felt like these people could live right down the street. Now, when we came back from intermission and got into act two, this is where I had a little bit of confusion. Act two is where the big revelation drops. The kind of twist that's supposed to reframe everything we've seen in the first act. And in many family dramas, this is the aha moment. I'm thinking of plays like Other Desert Cities or recently um on purpose on Broadway where the second act you get some new information or sur some revelation and suddenly you understand why everyone's been acting the way they have. But for me and the other Americans, the twist or the revelation wasn't really an aha moment. It was more of a oh. Instead of clarifying the character's behavior, it made me step back and try to puzzle out exactly what had happened. And while I was in my head trying to figure it out, I felt myself starting to detach from the drama playing out on stage. It's not that the revelation is uninteresting. On the contrary, it's definitely dramatic. But it didn't land for me in a way that really made perfect sense. and illuminated the family dynamic. It actually muddied the waters instead of sharpening them. And because of that, I found myself more observing the second act instead of being inside it emotionally, which is too bad because the actors are giving everything. Nelson's conflict was powerful. Patty had some heartbreaking moments. Nikki's struggle felt really raw, but I wasn't fully connecting because of the structure of the play had left me a little bit a drift. There were also a couple of character beats that didn't quite track for me. For example, Patty's reaction after this big revelation. She suddenly wants to kick Nelson out of the house and it felt like she was we were headed towards a divorce. Now, Patty has been written and played as a deeply supportive wife, someone who stood by Nelson for years despite his flaws. And so, that sudden flip felt abrupt, almost like it was serving the plot more than it was coming from the character we'd come to know thus far in the play. Moments like that took me out of it. Uh instead of feeling the emotional click, I was asking myself, would she really do that? Does this reaction line up with what we've seen? But let me be clear, none of this means that the play isn't worth seeing. Quite the opposite. The writing is alive. The characters are engaging. The performances are strong across the board. Nelson is a fascinating role. He's conflicted, ambitious, stubborn, flawed, and Leguisamo gives himself a complex character to wrestle with. Now, he isn't a very likable character, but that's not always a requirement for me. Patty and Norma are equally rich, and Nikki's struggles feel urgent and necessary to put on the stage. Structurally, I think the play could use another pass. Tightening the second act, sharpening the logic of the revelation, making sure that the characters reactions feel organic. But that's also part of the process with the new play. The foundation of this play is very strong and the talent involved is undeniable. I'm also keeping in mind that this is Leguamo's first multi- character play and it really is impressive for for the first time writing this kind of play. So, was I bored? No. The writing and performances keep me engaged the whole time. Was I confused? Yes. especially in the second act where the revelation didn't really land cleanly for me and some of the characters reaction felt unearned. But overall, The Other Americans is a worthwhile evening of theater. It's a significant step for John Leguisamo as a playwright, showing real skill with dialogue and character development in an ensemble context. I don't think this play will be heading to Broadway, but that makes this run even more special. If you want to see Leguisamo's work at this stage of its evolution and catch a cast of really talented actors, now is the time. So, tickets, there are $48 student tickets available at the box office with a student ID. And there on the Today Tix app, there are $48 rush tickets as well. So, now that's my take on the other Americans. Thanks for watching Bored and Confused. Don't forget to like, comment, and subscribe, and I will see you at the theater. Say hi if you see me. Don't want to drift away. Want to stay inside the flame. Keep me engaged. Keep me amused with what's in front of me. Cuz I don't want to be bored and confused.
